extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers, publishers, funders, and institutional research managers
extracted.subtask_short: preprint publishing and open peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed requirements for a publishing model that combines immediate public posting of preprints with a formal invited post-publication peer review process in biomedicine. Focuses on checks, referee selection and transparency, versioning, indexing, and article-level assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints provide a route for researchers to make their findings publicly available almost immediately – this removes the delay in when others can benefit from the new findings. It may also enable the authors to gain priority on the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints enable rapid dissemination and let authors gather informal comments from colleagues on possible problems and potential improvements before optionally committing to formal peer review at a journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing editorial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints remove editorial selection (beyond rapid checks for obvious nonsense), enabling a much broader range of findings to become visible that are currently difficult to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of work enabled by removal of selection include negative/null findings, advancements in protocols and methods, software articles, and data notes. Servers should still do rapid sanity checks similar to bioRxiv/arXiv/PeerJ Preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing author responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Because article preprints become visible with no prior editorial selection or judgement, and discussion can be visible to all, the onus is on the authors to take more care in the quality of the article before they post it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should ensure clarity, accuracy, and completeness prior to posting; public visibility and potential commentary create stronger incentives for authors to self-police quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for formal invited post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should have the option to publish immediately and then receive invited formal post-publication peer review to provide structured expert commentary to help authors improve presentation and to provide qualitative input for readers and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining preprints with invited formal post-publication review provides article-level qualitative assessment and can bypass non-transparent journal peer review that may censor or bias what becomes public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial rapid checks for posting
rubrics_metrics.description: All submitted articles that pass an initial rapid check are formally published (made public and citable) within a matter of days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial checks are similar to those of other major preprint servers and screen for obvious nonsense; there can be a preprint-only track for authors who do not commit to formal peer review immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor checks when moving into peer review track
rubrics_metrics.description: When authors choose formal peer review, the article is assessed more rigorously to include checks for readability, plagiarism, whether ethical standards have been adhered to, and ensuring supporting data/software and protocols have been included and deposited in a suitable format and repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These checks ensure material required for robust peer review and reproducibility is present before referees undertake formal assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting referees from a maintained expert panel
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors select referees from a large panel of experts (e.g., the F1000 Faculty); suggestions for other referees are checked by the panel to assess whether they should join.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintenance of expert groups and rules for joining could be overseen by an overarching board of researchers, institutions, societies, funders, etc., to ensure panel integrity and reduce bias or gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public declaration of conflicts by authors and referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Both authors and referees are required to publicly declare any conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict declarations should accompany the article and referee reports to promote transparency and trust in the assessment process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-driven, transparent refereeing process
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing is author-driven and transparent; referees provide a referee report and a status, which are both published immediately (following a quick check for appropriateness) alongside the article and the referee’s name and affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency of referee identity and reports is intended to remove biases that plague anonymous and optional-open peer review processes; reports and statuses should be published promptly after a light appropriateness check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and traceability for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees get credit for refereeing through citation of their report, capture of associated metrics, and linkage to their ORCID ID.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making referee outputs citable and linkable provides incentives for quality reviewing and allows reviewer contributions to be counted in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public commenting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who is a scientist can comment publicly on the article, as long as they provide their full name and affiliation, and declare any conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open commenting complements invited referee reports but requires identity and conflict transparency to reduce anonymous abuse and increase accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versioning and citable versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can respond publicly and can revise when they feel it is appropriate. New article versions are published and independently citable, but the latest version is the default visible on the site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older versions (HTML and PDF) should include clear information about the availability of newer versions, and a dynamic article citation should capture article version and refereeing status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing conditional on refereeing outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an article reaches a certain level of positive refereeing, it is included in PubMed and other major bibliographic indexers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexers should be updated with all future versions and referee reports; indexing thresholds and processes need to be defined so indexing reflects assessed quality rather than mere posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article-level qualitative assessment combined with other indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent invited post-publication peer review can provide a key source of qualitative article-level assessment to be combined with quantitative and qualitative indicators such as citation-based systems (e.g. RCR metrics), altmetrics, and expert recommendation services (e.g. F1000Prime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining multiple indicators provides a superior assessment compared with reliance on journal Impact Factor; systems should support aggregation of these different signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow preprint-only option and selective peer review suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may post their article without having to commit to formal post-publication peer review; some article types may not be appropriate for peer review or researchers may wish to get informal comments first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should provide flexible tracks (preprint-only vs. peer-review track) and clear guidance about which article types are suited to formal peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run experiments to evaluate the model
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of experiments should be conducted by the community where this approach is operated as a service on behalf of funders, institutions and researchers to test how well it fulfils the needs of biomedical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative trials will reveal unanticipated problems and allow the community to identify best practices and governance arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness relative to traditional publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: An open preprint-plus-invited-review system can be considerably cheaper than the current traditional publishing system (subscriptions or gold OA charges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost savings arise from removing selection and integrating transparent post-publication review; cost considerations should be part of evaluating new models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address low commenting rates with invited review
rubrics_metrics.description: Because it is hard to get much commentary on posted preprints (e.g., low rates of external comments observed on bioRxiv samples), formal invited review mechanisms are necessary to guarantee article-level qualitative input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on voluntary public comments is insufficient; an invited refereeing process ensures expert assessment is obtained.
